Entertainment.title: ‘It’s more than backcombing a beehive!’ How tribute acts got massive – and put the live music scene back in the black
Entertainment.text:
As peak heatwave sun beams down on to a field in Derbyshire, Amy Winehouse tells the crowd she is in need of hydration – so Robbie Williams fetches her a drink. Elsewhere, members of the public stop the Beastie Boys for selfies, Fred Durst grooves along as Diana Ross covers Al Green, and shirtless teenagers form a circle pit during Korn as a woman sits knitting in a camping chair just behind them. James Brown and Prince turn out to be the same artist – just dressed up in different clothes.

These are all scenes from Replika festival last month, which won the Guinness world record for the biggest tribute festival, with 108 acts performing across a very sweaty weekend. The punning deserves an accolade of its own: acts included Catfishing the Bottlemen, Pearl Scam, Wrong Jovi and Iffy Clyro.

It is far from the only event of its kind. The UK is inundated this summer, with Fake-Fest, Tribfest, Glastonbudget, Festwich, Tidal Gathering, Could Be Real and numerous others. Similarly, music venues across the country have listings crammed with tribute acts. Dave Bevan, managing director of Alive Network Entertainment Agency – which represents 234 such acts – estimates that there are between 3,000 and 5,000 outfits in operation in the UK.

The reason so many of these events and gigs are thriving is because going to see the original artist is often prohibitively expensive, especially during a cost of living crisis, while these gigs offer cheap access to live music, with songs you are guaranteed to know and love. Replika charges £100 for a weekend ticket. Its organiser, James Dean, says: “Our festival is targeted at low- to middle-income families who have very little disposable income. Compare that with the costs of going to Wembley Stadium for a single concert.” This is echoed by one group of young lads I speak to at the festival: “It’s cheap, local and a laugh.”

Dan Budd, who has performed as Robbie Williams for the last 14 years, is disarmingly good on stage, full of the requisite swagger and cheekiness, plus he has the same Stoke accent and even has matching real tattoos. “I don’t think I’ve ever been busier in terms of bookings,” he says. “I haven’t got a free Saturday night until September 2027.”

Dean tells me that the very top acts in the game will pull in £10,000-£15,000 a show. Budd won’t give me specific figures but says: “Put it this way, I’m 36 and mortgage-free.”

Similarly, Nadine l’Amour – who performs as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy – is flying. She set foot on stage as Winehouse for the first time in December 2024 but, by April 2025, she had quit her job as a secondary school teacher to do it full-time. Like Budd, L’Amour has replicated Winehouse’s tattoos, though she is such a fan that they were done years before she got into the tribute game.

“There are 14- and 15-year-old girls singing every single word,” she says of her shows. “I have young people saying: ‘I never got to see Amy, but watching you on stage, I feel like that’s the closest thing I’ll ever get.’”

It is not just individuals such as L’Amour and Budd who are benefiting. According to the charity Music Venue Trust (MVT), at a time when half the UK’s grassroots music venues make no profit, tribute artists are helping to keep the entire sector afloat.

“There is an elitist attitude about them, but these acts really do keep parts of the live music infrastructure moving,” says Nathan Clark, owner of the Brudenell Social Club in Leeds, one of the most well-respected and thoughtfully curated independent music venues in the country. Despite its buzzy reputation for cutting-edge newcomers and international indie stars, tribute bands play a significant role there. “Not every gig has to be about discovering the future,” he says. “The key is balance: tribute bands should support original music, not replace it.”

There is no hard data on the precise financial impact of tribute acts. MVT’s chief executive, Mark Davyd, guesses that they make up about 25-30% of all bookings in independent venues across the UK. The Night Time Industries Association also states there is no authoritative number, but a spokesperson says tribute acts contribute “many millions of pounds each year” to the live music industry.

Dean had an independent survey carried out on his festival’s economic impact over the last 10 years – including associated local spending on travel, hotels, supermarkets and so on – and it came out at about £8.5m. Given the number of touring tribute bands, festivals, gigs and events, he estimates a number that could stretch into hundreds of millions of pounds overall across the same 10-year span.

One reason this huge sector is being overlooked and undocumented is because it is often seen as a bit feeble or regressive. “People, especially in the mainstream music industry, look at us as nonstarters,” says Dean. “We’re not really taken seriously.” But tribute acts are no longer just dodgy Elvis impersonators with wayward pitch. “We’ve had a couple of Take That tributes who were able to sing a lot better than Robbie Williams and Gary Barlow,” says Dean; Clark points out that Graham Sampson of the Smyths, a Smiths tribute band, can probably hold a note better than Morrissey.

Such skill and dedication in mirroring others can bring with it an emotional toll. “Four or five years into it, I had a bit of a breakdown,” says Budd. “I couldn’t keep up with being one person in my private life and then going into Robbie mode and then having to switch it off again. It was like a split personality.” But Budd has found a way around it, performing a different set every night to keep it fresh, merging deep cuts with hits, and also being less gung-ho about inhabiting Williams. “As I’ve matured, I go on stage as Dan and I sing the songs in his style and manner,” he says.

When you love the act you are portraying, it can be more than just a gig. “There are a couple of songs that send me back to a time in my life that was quite dark,” says L’Amour. “Back to Black puts a very big lump in my throat when I sing that. It’s not only remembering my pain, but also the pain that Amy felt.” At Replika, L’Amour dedicates that song, very movingly, to a friend who has recently died. “As hard as it is to sing, it’s nice to dedicate that song to my friend who I lost to mental health,” she tells me later. “And that was also down to losing the person that she loved, and drinking and everything that was involved in that.”

L’Amour says that while some people – such as Replika’s Prince-James Brown combo – moonlight in numerous tribute acts, she could only ever do Winehouse because of the significance of the material. “This is more than sticking on eyeliner, backcombing the beehive and putting on really expensive, uncomfortable shoes,” she says. “It’s a feeling. That gut-wrenching first love that kicks you in the stomach; having your heart broken beyond repair. But then being able to pour that out to the audience and feeling that love come back. It’s way more than a tribute for me.”

Tribute acts also have a domino impact on other areas in the industry. “It may not always be treated as culturally prestigious but it creates employment,” Clark says. “It drives paying musicians, designers, promoters, venues.” He points to the Smyths having a four-night run coming up at his venue. “What original bands at this grassroots level can do four nights and sell them out?” he asks. “Very few. Those four shows allow us to take the risk on booking something else.”

Tribute bands also tend to bring in “exponentially higher” bar revenue for venues, according to Davyd, as gigs are usually held at the weekend and are often attended by groups of people. Clark agrees: “A tribute show is often more of a social night out: people are relaxed, they know the songs, they sing together … it’s like a celebration. For independent venues, that matters. Bar income is a major part of how grassroots venues survive.”

Davyd points out that tribute acts “fill up the programme” in smaller towns “where there is an absence of touring acts”, which is a mixed blessing. Yes, they allow people to see live music in places bigger acts ignore, but does their success make it harder for acts starting out who are writing and performing their own material? “Any experience with live music is really important for social interaction, community cohesion and a whole bunch of reasons,” he says. “But we really need to be concerned about generating the next wave of great British talent. I would prefer there was more space for that. Tribute bands are an important part of the grassroots sector but we wouldn’t like them to become the sole reason venues are open.”

What is clear at Replika festival is that while, for many, these bands are vehicles for pure nostalgia, comfort and familiarity – big Oasis choruses, indelible Beatles hooks and sugary 00s pop – they are also a first gateway to music. It is genuinely endearing watching battle-jacket-clad children navigating their first mosh pit and working out the rhythms and etiquette, as a fake Limp Bizkit turns a sizeable tent into an explosion of bouncing bodies. And it is a dream come true for the band members, too, who seem blown away by the response. The turntablist shouts out to his parents in the audience, his adrenaline clearly pumping, as he declares: “They keep telling me to get a real job – but look at me now!”

Entertainment.title: Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G film
Entertainment.text:
The Wimbledon lawn tennis championships are not generally a hotbed of crime. Yet this year, unprecedented infringements ocurred. Eleven players were fined a total of £34,000 for “audible obscenities” and “racquet abuse”. Meanwhile, a spectator at the men’s singles final called a heckler a “bumbaclat” before inviting them to fight, badgered Prince William to repay a drugs debt of £1,400 allegedly owed to him by Prince Harry from his days at Eton, and attempted to sell illegal substances to those seated near him – and beyond. “If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed,” he posted on Instagram, touting for business, “I iz here wif de hookup.”

The culprit was Ali G, real name Alistair Leslie Graham, AKA the malapropism-dropping home counties wide boy played by Sacha Baron Cohen, kitted out for the occasion in trademark skullcap and gold chain, plus custom Wimbledon jacket, traditional crossed rackets replaced with cannabis leaves. Security released him without penalty, but the reprimand was captured on scores of smartphones – including one held by Cohen himself.

Such footage is likely to find its way into a movie that will be released worldwide on 23 October and whose existence was only revealed four days before the Wimbledon incident. This week, a title was announced – Ali G: Who Iz I? – as well as the fact the film is to be the directorial debut of its star: a new development in the career of one of the UK’s most audacious, ambitious – and powerful – comedy actors, apparently taking greater agency over his projects as his own political engagement intensifies. (The appalled reaction to his recent Netflix comedy Ladies First, which he neither wrote nor directed, suggests this is a sage move.)

It also makes sense logistically: Ali G is a character who would energetically embrace selfie-mode shooting, which presumably streamlines a film crew considerably. Meanwhile the absence of a US theatrical release for the first Ali G film, 2002’s Indahouse, means targets in America would be easier to hoodwink.

Cohen first rose to fame as the tracksuit-wearing naïf and committed cultural appropriator in 1998, when Ali G was introduced as the “voice of the yoof” on Channel 4’s The 11 O’Clock Show. His own show followed in the early 2000s, constructed around interviews with unsuspecting subjects including Buzz Aldrin (whom he called Buzz Lightyear and asked if he was “ever jealous of Louis Armstrong”), Naomi Wolf (whom he complimented by telling her she’s attractive enough to be a sex worker) and Tony Benn. The late MP was outraged by the character’s dismissal of striking workers in 1984 as lazy skivers; Cohen later told Benn he was the only interviewee who had “dealt seriously with his loud, sexist, materialist image of youth”. (Benn’s letter of reply ended with the words: “You’re my main man.”)

Although Cohen declared both Ali G and Borat – his Kazakh TV presenter and the star of a 2006 film that was a commercial and critical hit – retired in 2007, both have since returned. Borat was resurrected in 2020, for Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, intended by Baron Cohen as an intervention in the impending US presidential election. As with his 2018 series Who is America?, it secured a number of high-profile and highly-embarrassing scalps – most notably Rudy Giuliani, who was caught with his hand down his trousers in a hotel room with an actor pretending to be Borat’s 15-year-old daughter.

Before his recent reappearance, Ali G was last seen presenting an award at the 2016 Oscars: a surprise even to the show’s producers, who understood Cohen would appear as himself. The ruse involved the star feigning food poisoning then locking himself and then-wife Isla Fisher in a disabled loo for 40 minutes to change into his costume.

While Ali G Indahouse was a scripted comedy concerning the character’s inadvertent role in the downfall of the government, indications are that its sequel will be closer to the more politically intentional Borat followup, returning Ali G to his origins as an interviewer whose dubious views prompt his subjects to reveal their own.

The film was shot in secret – as was 2009’s Brüno, in which Baron Cohen skewered the fashion industry – but some of the leaked locations in the UK and US give early clues as to whom Cohen may have had in his crosshairs.

Last summer, there were sightings of the character in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire - home to the likes of David Cameron, Rebekah Brooks, Ellen DeGeneres and Jeremy Clarkson. The town was also, during the dates Ali G was spotted, playing host to US vice president JD Vance and his family, there to enjoy a Cotswolds holiday.

Vance travelled with a considerable security detail, so it remains uncertain how close Cohen would have been able to get, had he been in pursuit. The Sun ran a photograph of the character sporting a Rastafarian beret while filming at a nearby wildlife park in Burford. A source told the paper: “He was with a whole film crew and was in full character. He seemed very comfortable in the role. I was amazed, I thought to myself, ‘that’s Ali G’.”

A crew member on the film to whom the Guardian spoke said an NDA prevented them from comment, but added: “I CAN tell you that it’s gonna be big. And packed full of laughs.”

Representatives for Kellie Bright, Charles Dance and Martin Freeman, all of who had roles in the original film, did not respond to enquiries, but the actor Adam Deacon confirmed he was not returning, “even though I would have loved to be a part of it”. He added that he could also do a “perfect” Borat accent so would be happy to be kept in mind for further films featuring that character too. “I’m a massive fan of what Sacha creates and I hope the new movie is a success.”

In the first film, Deacon played a member of the East Staines Massiv, the rivals of Ali G’s less-than-intimidating gang from the other end of town. The Surrey commuter town was sceptical about the fame bestowed on it by the Ali G connection, and in 2010, a group spearheaded by the Spelthorne business forum lobbied the borough council to change the town’s name to Staines-upon-Thames in an attempt to add distance. The area, said Alex Tribick, chair of the forum at the time, “is really rather nice and it has some fantastic natural beauty around it”.

He added: “Staines has had some adverse press further to that with it being portrayed as an urban wasteland off the end of the M25. The purpose of the exercise is to improve the image of Staines, rebrand it, and denote its greatest natural resource.”

The then MP for Spelthorne, Kwasi Kwarteng, supported the move – which was duly voted through by the local council in 2011 – saying “if anyone knows anything about Staines, then one would know that Ali G is a million miles from it. It’s a very charming place actually.”

Yet in his Thursday video announcing the title and release date, Ali G announces himself as “representing the westside of Staines-upon-Thames” – suggesting the area is unlikely to shake off the association any time soon.

Happily, the sitting Spelthorne MP, Lincoln Jopp, said he welcomed news of the return of the town’s prodigal son. “I can’t believe Ali G is coming back!” he said. “I loved Ali G Indahouse; it’s hilarious. Sacha Baron Cohen is a genius.”

Jopp, who specified to the Guardian that his constituency includes the “West Staines Massiv”, added that the town was “a great place. We can take a bit of mickey-taking, trust me. Booyakasha!”

Posts on local Facebook forums suggest resurgent grassroots support for the character putting the town on the map. “Oh happy days, loved the film,” wrote Blossom Welch, while longtime Staines resident Joanna Barlow added: “Loved Ali G not ashamed saw the show being filmed thought it was hilarious.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today Programme.

"We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

"We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13.

"However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Handing down the judgement, Justice Julian Goose said: "Many who have heard the evidence might describe what he did as evil, who could dispute it?"

He added: "I am sure Rudakubana had the settled determination to carry out these offences and had he been able to, he would have killed each and every child - all 26 of them."

The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about his past mental health conditions.

Rudakubana was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

In May 2025 there was an investigation after Rudakubana allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water.

Under the Mental Health Act, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The law requires he be transferred back to prison when he no longer requires treatment in hospital. His sentence is not being converted into a "hospital order", which would mean he stayed at Broadmoor.

Confirming the transfer on Thursday, the MoJ said the families of those murdered and injured would be in the country's heart forever and "our thoughts remain with them" and said it does not change Rudakubana's sentence.

A statement continued: "Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act.

"Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tens of thousands evacuated from France's Cap Ferret peninsula as wildfires spread
BreakingNewsTab.text:
French authorities have ordered the evacuation of the entirety of the Cap Ferret peninsula on the south-west coast, with hundreds of people escaping the area by boat.

Tens of thousands of people are being evacuated from the tourism destination west of Bordeaux, as firefighters continue to battle what the local prefect has described as an "XXL fire" in the Gironde region.

The fires, which began on Tuesday, have burned for days, with officials saying 10,000 hectares (almost 25,000 acres) had been consumed by the flames.

Meanwhile, the government in Spain has declared a national emergency as wildfires burn out of control in several areas close to the capital Madrid.

Responding to the spread of fires, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the president of the community of Madrid, said it was: "The worst fire in the history of the region."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke of a "dramatic situation" and urged people to take great care. Three fires were burning west of Madrid, at Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 40,000 people had either been or were in the process of being evacuated from the Cap Ferret peninsula, which has the Atlantic on one side and the Bay of Arcachon on the other.

Local prefect Sophie Brocas said 53 homes had been lost as well as a campsite, but that 2,000 houses had been saved.

A local councillor said 2,000 evacuees from the peninsula had already arrived by boat in the port of Arcachon on the south side of the bay.

Fire and rescue chief Marc Vermeulen said the wildfire had spread rapidly at the end of Thursday and into the early hours of Friday. Authorities then took the decision on Friday morning to begin the evacuation of the town of Arès, which lies south-east of Lège-Cap Ferret on the Bay of Arcachon.

Vermeulen compared the fires overnight to those in 2022 - explaining the area is in a more severe state of drought now.

While in 2022, fires were "exploding" at the end of the day and the nights were favourable for firefighting, in the current fires they are exploding during the night at midnight or 01:00.

"When I say explosion, it means that for several hours, we had propagation speeds on the order of 800 to 1,000 hectares burned per hour, in the context of a suburban area."

Further down the Atlantic coast, around the town of Biscarrosse in France's Landes region, another major fire that began on Thursday afternoon has prompted the evacuations of more than 23,000 people.

About 18,000 people in Biscarrosse and 5,000 in Parentis-en-Born had to leave their homes, campsites, a nursing home and a summer camp.

Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said the fire around Biscarrosse was not going to be out by the end of Friday, with winds of up to 50km/h (31mph) and temperatures of 36-37C.

He added that 105 homes and other buildings had so far been identified as either partially or completely destroyed by the flames.

No further casualties have been reported overnight in south-west France, although two firefighters died on Tuesday while tackling a blaze near Bordeaux airport.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday night the wildfire situation in the country was "very tense" - especially in the Gironde region.

The European Union has sent three planes and two helicopters to help the French fire effort, and another four planes to Spain.

Headmaster David Morton, 53, from Gloucester had been on holiday with his wife and sons when they received an emergency alert via text overnight on Thursday instructing them to evacuate.

The family were staying in a house in Petit Piquey, along the peninsula, and were woken up at 03:00 local time (01:00 GMT) by emergency texts and an alert on the property's landline.

"Everyone was driving with their lights on, driving very slowly – there was lots of fire service people, ambulances, police on the other side of the road controlling things and we could see several fires in the distance as we drove," he told the BBC.

"It's different from seeing it on the television… seeing it blazing out of control despite hundreds and hundreds of firemen and women helping."

Olivia Jarratt, 44, was evacuated from Truc Vert campsite on the peninsula with her husband and two children in the early hours of Friday morning.

Her daughter was woken with sirens and the family left their tent, camping gear and bikes behind as they made the drive to Bordeaux.

"At first, we dismissed it, and thought she was having a nightmare, but we realised it was all going on, and everyone was packing in a panic. There's only one road off the peninsula, so people were trying to be as quick as possible.

"There was a loudspeaker with the sirens, but obviously that was in French, and with everything, we couldn't understand what was happening."

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. That rapid rise in temperatures is making its summers hotter and, particularly in the south, drier.

The hotter, drier conditions leave soils, trees and other vegetation with less moisture, creating the fuel in which wildfires can take hold. A spark is still needed - most often from human activity, usually accidental but sometimes deliberate, or from lightning.

Once a fire starts, extreme heat, dry vegetation and strong winds can help it spread faster, burn more intensely and become much harder to control.

How forests and landscapes are managed also matters: accumulated vegetation and abandoned land can provide more fuel for fires. But the European Environment Agency has said "climate change has increased forest fire risk across Europe", with the greatest danger expected in southern Europe.

Additional reporting by BBC climate editor Justin Rowlatt.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Carrickmacross: Police 'intercept car with bomb on way to attack in NI'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A car containing an "extremely significant" bomb has been intercepted in the Republic of Ireland as it was being driven across the border for an attack in Northern Ireland, Irish police have said.

The vehicle was stopped during an operation targeting dissident republican activities on Wednesday but further details are just emerging. Two people were arrested.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed on Friday that officers found an explosive device and described it as an "extremely significant seizure".

The vehicle was stopped on the N2 near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, at about 15:00 local time on Wednesday.

A woman in her 20s, who was the driver of the vehicle, was arrested on Wednesday afternoon and a man in his 40s has since been arrested.

Irish broadcaster RTÉ has reported that gardaí (Irish police) sources said the bomb contained a power unit, a detonator and military grade explosives.

Gardaí sources also said it was expected to be used as a under-car bomb in an attack in Northern Ireland, according to RTÉ.

Speaking to reporters in County Tipperary, Kelly said: "Any seizure of this nature is really concerning.

"However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday Agreement, they did not put weapons and explosives (out of use), they didn't, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning.

"So that is something that we continue to deal with.

"There's a small minority of these individuals, I would describe them as radicalised republicans, and this is a threat that we're going to continue to face for some time."

Kelly said that the bomb was "not just components or pieces".

"This was an explosive device and it would have or could have potentially caused significant damage.

"This is an intelligence-led operation, so we certainly do have information in relation to the individuals involved."

Ireland's Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan described the seizure as "very worrying".

"I think it evidences the fact that there is an ongoing threat in respect of dissident republican activity," he said.

The minister added: "I suppose what I'm encouraged about is that the gardaí were able to apprehend the suspect.

"The device has been defused. I want to commend the gardaí for the work they did in ensuring that this didn't become a real threat to the public."

O'Callaghan said it was "obvious" that "a very serious criminal act" would have occurred if police had not intercepted the suspects.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant thanked Irish police for their "quick, decisive action".

"Intercepting a dangerous device like this undoubtedly saved lives and kept communities safe on both sides of the border. Strong cross-border security cooperation remains as vital as ever."

PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said he welcomed the "significant seizure and the arrests" made by Irish police, who he said they work with "very closely on a daily basis".

"This underlines our joint commitment to address the threat posed by violent dissident republican groups and keep communities safe.

"We will continue to liaise closely with An Garda Síochána in relation to their investigation, and provide any support as required," he said.

The term "dissident republicans" describes a range of individuals who do not accept the Good Friday Agreement - the 1998 peace deal which ended the worst of the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

The Provisional IRA - the main armed republican paramilitary group for most of the Troubles - declared a ceasefire in the run up to the agreement and officially ended its violent campaign in 2005.

Dissident republicanism is made up of various groups which broke away from the Provisional IRA in the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s, including the Continuity IRA and New IRA.

The groups are much smaller than the Provisional IRA, although they have access to high-calibre weapons and have used improvised explosive devices and mortars in attacks and attempted attacks.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
BreakingNewsTab.text:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again.

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032, this is a live question.

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

Let's see.

BreakingNewsTab.title: They became best friends - then discovered they were brother and sister
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Dave Green and Andrea Urmston found they instantly hit it off when their paths crossed while working in separate roles at Manchester Airport.

The two strangers got on so well they could complete each other's sentences - which made sense when they discovered the truth.

Dave was Andrea's biological brother, but had been adopted by another family when he was a baby.

"I was shaking, I was just shaking and my heart was pounding," Andrea told the BBC. "I'd finally found him. It's unbelievable."

In 2005, Dave was managing the bus station at the airport and Andrea serviced the vending machines.

Over the next two years they became firm friends, texting and phoning each other when they were not at work.

One day during a phone call, Dave told Andrea something he had never mentioned before. He was adopted and his birth name was Stuart Proudlove.

"I kind of froze and didn't speak for a minute," said Andrea.

Her maiden name was Proudlove and she had a brother who was adopted before she was born.

"It's not a very popular name and it had to be him. Other than family, I had never heard that surname anywhere else," she added.

She immediately rang her mother, Susan, to check her long-lost brother's birth date. They matched: 24 March 1966. She called Dave straight back.

"I said 'it's got to be you, it's got to be you', and I said 'I need to see you', and so I went to pick him up," Andrea said.

As they were driving to their mother's house, Dave realised where he was. They were driving along the bus route he used to cover before becoming a manager.

His old route had taken him right past his mother's house, and the school that Andrea had attended.

He had been within touching distance of his birth family without realising.

Susan said finally meeting Dave was a surreal moment.

"There were lots of tears. Then we just all hugged," said Andrea.

"I couldn't believe that I'd got my brother and my mum together, it was amazing."

Andrea's mother had told her that she had a brother when she was younger.

She told her he had been given up for adoption and had gone to a lovely lady who could not have children of her own.

"I immediately wanted to go and call him so we could play," Andrea said.

Susan said she had tried to find her son with the help of the Salvation Army, but had not got anywhere.

"I asked if we could go and get him back," Andrea said. "She did explain that it didn't work that way, so I promised her that I would find him for her one day."

Now they were finally being reunited.

"She had wanted that since being as young as I can remember," Andrea added.

"So yeah, I gave her that. I promised her that."

On the mantlepiece in Susan's home was a picture of Dave as a baby.

It had been sent by his adopted parents to his birth mother days after his adoption.

The same photograph had also been displayed in his adopted parents' house.

Dave had known since he was 10 that he was adopted, because his adoptive parents had shown him the paperwork.

But he said he had a very happy childhood, and had never harboured any desire to track down his birth mother.

"I didn't feel like I had to go searching or have any unanswered questions," he added.

For all three, finding each other has been a life-changing experience.

"I went from having really not a lot of positivity in my life at the time, to finding out that my best friend was my sister," Dave said.

"I'd found my birth mum being able to sort of make her truly happy. And I'd found a family really that I never really knew existed."

Their mother died recently, but both said they were glad she got to be reunited with her son.

"She was so desperate to find you to make sure you'd had a really good life," Andrea said.

For Andrea, the reunion was bittersweet. She had longed to find her brother for years.

"My mum and dad, they separated unfortunately and so I went through a lot of hard times knowing [Dave] was out there but I didn't know [where]."

The pair said they were now making the most of the time they have together after moving in with each other in Kidsgrove, Staffordshire.

Finding each other was, they said, their "lottery win".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Four men killed in Huyton, Merseyside, as car hits lamp-post
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Four men have died after a car hit a lamp-post on Merseyside, police have said.

The car left the road and crashed on Liverpool Road, Huyton, just before 02:00 BST.

The men, two aged 23, and two others, aged 24 and 26 died at the scene, Merseyside Police said.

A 27-year-old man who was a passenger inside the vehicle has been taken to hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

The black Seat Cupra had been travelling from Liverpool towards Knowsley before it came off the road and hit the lamp-post.

Eleven roads in the area have been closed, including Liverpool Road and East Prescot Road, from the junction of Princess Drive and Finch Lane while police carry out their investigations.

The closures are likely to remain in place over the weekend, the force said.

Supt Paul Holden of Merseyside Police said the force's priority was to get answers for the families of those affected over how the crash occurred.

He said: "We know this happened very early this morning, but if anyone saw what happened or were driving through the area just before the incident occurred then please get in touch."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

Swinging typically involves couples meeting up and exchanging partners, but it can also involve just one half of a couple having sexual encounters while their partner watches. Many people take part fully consensually.

Some of the women who got in touch accuse FabSwingers of facilitating abuse and failing to tackle illegal behaviour.

The site says it has moderation policies and is not "responsible for private off-platform conduct between adults".

"We do not accept any suggestion that FabSwingers is indifferent to misuse," it added.

But the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Labour MP Jess Phillips, believes FabSwingers "should be shut down".

Police should recognise coercion or pressure to take part in swinging as a form of adult sexual exploitation, she says. "Calling it swinging implies consent, and therefore puts the blame at the feet of the women, and that makes it silencing for those women."

Experts have told BBC News it is important to understand that people can be manipulated into consent. Partners who pressure women into swinging can then use the resulting shame as a means of control, they say.

The Swingers podcast and our previous article told the story of Ruth O'Grady, who said her ex-husband would arrange for her to have sex with other men, sometimes as many as four in a single day. She says she went along with it to keep him happy. Her ex-husband has not responded to BBC News's questions.

The backgrounds and relationships of the women who contacted us in response to Ruth's story are all different - but many said her honesty had given them permission to talk about their own abuse, kept hidden for years.

One woman said, had she not seen our reporting, she "probably would have had sex against my will literally this evening. This has been my situation for 12 years now." The abuse will take place "no more", she said.

Another woman, Emily from Derbyshire, said she had been pushed into going to a swinging club while pregnant. "That was my baby girl," she said of her daughter. "It feels awful that I mixed her up in it."

Emily had hoped a single visit would be enough, but she said her husband wanted more, and they ended up joining FabSwingers. For years, evenings became consumed by searching the site for hook-ups.

If their young daughter had not fallen asleep by 7pm, Emily said her husband would come into the bedroom and pull her away saying: "Mummy's got to go now."

Emily said her daughter would cry because she was not ready to say goodnight, or because they had not finished the bedtime story.

She eventually left the marriage but estimates she had sex with between 20 and 30 men while swinging.

She did not think of it as sexual abuse at the time, she told us, because she had agreed to try swinging. She does now.

Sixteen users told us they had reported to police either alleged abuse or the posting of intimate images on FabSwingers without consent. Three said this had led to convictions.

However, 10 raised concerns about the way police had handled their cases.

One woman said she was 21 when her boyfriend put her on FabSwingers. He ran the whole profile, she told us, and she does not even know the identity of some of the men she had sex with because her boyfriend would make sure she could not see them or talk to them.

She went to the police but they eventually dropped her case. She says they told her she looked like she had been enjoying the sex in the videos they had viewed.

The woman said she explained to officers that her ex-boyfriend would be angry if she did not look enthusiastic enough and make her have sex with someone else.

"The police made me feel like I was disgusting," she said.

Details of organisations offering information about or support after sexual abuse or with feelings of despair are available at bbc.co.uk/actionline

Police need better training to understand coercive control and how pressure to engage in sexual acts can form part of domestic abuse, says Dame Nicole Jacobs, domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales.

The National Police Chiefs Council told the BBC: "Victims deserve to be listened to and supported consistently across the country."

One woman who contacted us said she felt she could not go to the police because her husband was a serving police officer.

Susie, whose name we have changed, said he talked for years about his fantasy of her having sex with other men - and eventually persuaded her to join FabSwingers.

She described one meet where her husband sat on a sofa in a hotel room and just watched her have sex with a stranger - a practice known as "hotwifing".

The next man her husband wanted her to have sex with was a fellow police officer he worked with, said Susie.

The whole swinging experience broke her, she told us: "I wasn't sleeping. I was drinking so much every night." She is now getting divorced and taking antidepressants.

Eleven men also got in touch with their experiences of having used FabSwingers.

One described arriving at a house for sex, arranged through the website, and finding a woman naked on a bed. A phone was "propped up on the side and a male voice was telling her what to do next", explained the man.

He and the woman then had sex, he said, and the man at the end of line "wanted evidence of it, by me holding the phone up close to show him". The woman "had no say on what went down at all".

It was only when he listened to the Swingers podcast, that he considered she was potentially being controlled and abused, he said. He now regrets what happened.

This is concerning, Jess Phillips told us: "Not even training your moderators on your website. They should be ashamed of themselves."

Unlike some other swinging sites, FabSwingers does not require identity verification, which can make it harder for police to identify suspects when allegations are reported. It also means a banned user can create a new account - although FabSwingers says it can detect this, without explaining how it does so.

FabSwingers told the BBC its moderation processes involve up to five site administrators, who moderators report to, alongside AI and "automated controls".

Since 2023, the website has been mentioned in at least 329 police reports across the UK - according to Freedom of Information requests submitted by the BBC - including in allegations of rape, sexual offences, coercive control, harassment, blackmail, stalking, assault and possession of extreme pornography. Although, it does not mean FabSwingers was responsible for what was alleged in the reports.

Jess Phillips said she believes the site "falls foul" of the Online Safety Act, adding she would encourage the regulator Ofcom "to look into it very, very seriously right now and shut it down".

Ofcom says it is "extremely concerned" to hear of the BBC's findings and is speaking to the site's provider, but it has not so far launched an investigation.

The vast majority of those contacting the BBC were women who wanted to thank Ruth O'Grady, the subject of the Swingers podcast, for sharing her story.

"I'm still not in a place where I want anyone I love to know some of these things about my past," one woman told us. "But I feel a little less alone now."

BreakingNewsTab.title: US hits dozens of countries with new wave of tariffs
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The US has imposed new tariffs on 60 trading partners in the latest escalation in the trade war reignited by US President Donald Trump when he returned to office last year.

Those targeted, including the UK, China and the European Union, will face a tariff of 10% to 12.5% on all goods, accounting for almost all American imports.

The tariffs, which replace an identical levy which expires on Friday, are based on claims key economic partners have failed to properly tackle forced labour.

But US trade expert Caroline Freund said the move is "not about forced labour" but that Trump is simply "looking for a legal reason to put the tariffs in".

The US Supreme Court had ruled earlier this year that many of the tariffs imposed globally under emergency powers were illegally enacted.

The 10%-12.5% duties on imports were proposed last month by the White House and over concerns they were not doing enough to tackle forced labour.

"Today's action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said.

The new duties apply to the top 60 US trade partners covering 99.4% of US imports, the Office of the US Trade Representative said.

The new tariffs were a "like for like" swap with the regime that expired on Friday, Freund, Dean of the UC San Diego School of Global Policy and Strategy, told the BBC's Today programme.

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?

Asked about the forced labour justification, she said: "I think they were looking for a legal reason to put the tariffs in and that they can maintain them because their goals and Greer has been very clear about this, as has Trump, is about the trade deficit and it is about US manufacturing, it is not about forced labour."

The levies are likely to raise costs for businesses and consumers, although its impact could be softened due to the number of exempted goods, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's economic security expert Wendy Cutler.

She added most trading partners would be disappointed with the new levies and were likely to focus on ways to "reduce their dependence on the US" by making deals with other countries.

The head of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said the UK had lost its comparative advantage against the European Union as a result of the new tariffs.

William Bain told the BBC the EU has a 10% all-inclusive deal for tariffs on its goods, while the UK is facing 10% universal tariffs on top of any duties imposed on individual goods.

"So there will be some concerns in the business community this morning about what the UK needs to do to get the same treatment the European Union has got here," Bain added.

David Henig, director of UK trade policy at the European Centre for International Political Economy, also noted the UK's relative disadvantage compared with the EU.

He told Today: "We have slightly moved backwards, but this is President Trump so anything could change tomorrow or the day after.

"I don't think too many businesses will be changing their plans based on that."

Trump has long argued that tariffs protect American workers and boost the US economy.

In April 2025, Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50% on global trading partners on what he called "Liberation Day", aiming to address what he saw as unfair treatment of the US.

In February, the US Supreme Court struck down those tariffs and said the president had exceeded his authority, prompting tens of billions of dollars in refunds.

But the White House has since looked at alternative ways to impose import duties, including a sweeping 10% levy as part of a temporary solution that expired on Friday.

Washington has also imposed other tariffs on countries such as Brazil and Canada.

The US and China have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Trump has used tariffs to press countries, such as Mexico, on non-trade issues.

The administration could be set to impose further tariffs as it is currently investigating 16 countries - accounting for the vast majority of US imports - over claims of manufacturing overcapacity.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Heat health alerts in effect as rain returns this weekend
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Yellow heat health alerts came into effect across central and southern England on Friday morning with temperatures forecast to reach 30C (86F) in places.

The alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the East and West Midlands, eastern England, London, south-east England and south-west England and are valid from 09:00 BST on Friday until 09:00 on Sunday.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

It comes as parts of the UK prepare to see much-needed rain this weekend - although amounts are expected to be relatively small, especially in the south.

A drought was officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales on Thursday.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in "prolonged dry weather" category - one stage below a drought - and the Sottish Environment Protection Agency said much of eastern Scotland has moved into 'water scarcity' status

Hosepipe bans are in force for millions of the customers across eastern and southern England.

North-westerly winds that have developed over recent days will briefly be cut off in southern areas on Friday, allowing temperatures to climb.

Central, southern and eastern parts of England will widely reach highs of 25-28C (77-82F), with a few spots expected to reach 30C.

Parts of east Wales could also climb into the high 20s, with other locations in Wales and northern England forecast to see 20-25C (68-77F).

It will be rather warm in Northern Ireland and Scotland too with afternoon highs reaching 19-23C.

Most areas will see sunny spells although thick cloud will linger in north-west Scotland with patchy rain arriving during Friday afternoon.

Temperatures will slowly drop over the weekend as fresher north-westerly winds return.

By Sunday afternoon highs will range from 16C (61F) in northern Scotland to 25C (77F) in south-east England.

It is expected to bring an end to the heatwave conditions that have persisted for 19 days so far at Usk in Monmouthshire and Exeter in Devon.

High pressure will retreat to the west allowing weather fronts to move south-eastwards across the UK which will bring some outbreaks of rain over the weekend.

Rainfall amounts could be reasonably significant over high ground in the north and the west of the UK, with 20mm (0.8in) possible in parts of north-west Scotland.

However, the wet weather is expected to be much patchier further south and east with large swathes of England and Wales forecast to see just a few millimetres at most.

It is likely that locations in the south will see little rain, if any.

Wisley in Surrey has now gone well over a month without any wet weather and it is by no means certain that it will record any rainfall on Friday or this weekend.

Either way, it is unlikely to bring much of an improvement for the large parts of England and Wales that are officially in drought - or just one step away - as a result of prolonged dry spells during spring and summer so far.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK complacent about war threat, warns BAE Systems' boss
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK has been too complacent about the risk of foreign attack, the boss of Europe's biggest defence contractor BAE Systems has warned.

Dr Charles Woodburn told the BBC in an exclusive interview that the level of threat was the highest he'd seen in his lifetime.

He welcomed the recent boost to defence spending but said much more would be needed to hit the government's commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

He also warned we were not far from the use of autonomous lethal weapons by countries that may not follow the UK's policy of maintaining human control.

In a rare interview, Woodburn told the BBC the reality of modern warfare had "changed quite profoundly" and that UK defence spending had to change with it.

He said Russia and Ukraine had become "incredibly adept" at using autonomy in the form of drones and counter drones.

"It's something that we now have to really understand and make sure that we're able to provide the capabilities that can counter that and deter aggression," he said.

BAE Systems unveiled a life-size model of an unmanned fighter jet in front of the new Defence Secretary Wes Streeting at the Farnborough International Air Show.

Four of these so-called Collaborative Combat Aircraft will accompany a manned fighter to massively increase firepower but at just 20% of the cost of a piloted aircraft.

However, Woodburn said there was still a role for the traditional battleships and submarines that BAE has been manufacturing for decades.

"If you look at what our adversaries are building, they're also building significantly large platforms - aircraft, ships, submarines. And they're supplemented by some of these unmanned capabilities." It is the combination of the two that has the "winning" formula, he said.

It is hardly surprising that the boss of a defence company would like to see more defence spending. But Woodburn said the UK had been complacent for some time about the level of threat it faced - particularly from Russia.

"This is by far the most threatening time I've seen," he said. "Even when I joined the company in 2016 I was amazed at what we saw Russian submarines doing, the cyber attacks. I think that's come a long way sadly as a result of the Ukraine conflict we're much more aware of the proximity of a hot war in Europe."

The war readiness of the UK's armed forces has been questioned by senior armed services figures and openly mocked by the US. General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, recently said the navy is not ready for war.

Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary sarcastically referred to the "big bad Royal Navy" while President Donald Trump described the UK's aircraft carriers as "toys".

That impression was not helped by the tardiness of mobilising the destroyer HMS Dragon – built by BAE - to provide air cover for Cyprus against Iranian and Hezbollah threats.

Woodburn insisted the company had responded as soon as the Ministry of Defence had asked for its help.

He said BAE gets "things in place as quickly as we're able to but at the end of the day you need a signal to move".

Woodburn welcomed the promotion of former Defence Secretary John Healey to chancellor. Healey very publicly resigned from the post insisting that the extra money awarded to defence "falls well short of what is needed to protect the country".

An additional £13.5bn was boosted to an extra £15bn after he resigned but that will only bring spending on defence to 2.68% of GDP by 2030 – well short of the 3% Healey said was required. A further massive increase in spending will be needed to hit the government goal of 3.5% by 2035.

Shares in defence companies – including BAE – rose on the news that Healey was moving into number 11 but Woodburn knows he will have other departments competing for cash.

"We have tremendous respect for John," he said. "He understands what is needed and I think in that sense its very good he's in the Treasury role."

He recognised Healey would have a host of complicated national finances to tackle. "But the fact that he understands the requirements of defence we see as a very positive thing", he said.

The UK's armed forces have dwindled since the end of the cold war. In 1990 – the army had 153,000 regular soldiers. Today that number is just 74,000.

But it is debatable how many human soldiers you need these days and Woodburn said a new era of autonomous lethal weaponry was close at hand.

"We're not far from that. While we follow rules of 'man in the loop' we know very well that our adversaries are not always doing that," he said.

At the air show, new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham sent a video with a message that defence could play a big role in his plans to reindustrialise the economy and provide thousands of skilled jobs.

And in his keynote speech at the airshow Streeting said: "Defence will not just be a recipient of the proceeds of economic growth. It will be a central contributor to building that growth, a driver of prosperity in parts of the country that are crying out for the backing they need to make their contribution to the challenge of our time."

Woodburn said he wanted to help make the case for the knock-on benefits of defence spending.

"We need to make sure that the industrial benefits, the jobs benefits are well told so people understand this is money well spent," he said.

But does he ever lose sleep over the fact that his products are ultimately intended to kill people?

"The thing I always think about is that the best thing we can do is to deter. Detering war means our brave men and women have the best kit they could possibly have. Our mission as a business is to protect those who protect us and we take that incredibly seriously."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Oil prices hit $100 for the first time since May
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May as the escalating conflict in the Middle East reignited fears over global energy supplies.

Brent crude - the global benchmark for oil prices - rose more than 6% on Thursday following several days of increases as the US stepped up military strikes against Iran.

Prices spiked after Houthi militia in Yemen attacked oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a key export route that Saudi Arabia has used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

Gas prices have also risen steadily over the past month, with the benchmark UK gas price currently at around 150 per therm, up from around 98p at the end of June.

Oil prices had been falling following a temporary ceasefire between the US and Iran.

They dropped back to levels last seen before the US and Israel began military action against Iran on 28 February.

However, the ceasefire has failed and this week US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the people in charge in Iran were "not ready to make a deal".

The ongoing conflict risks pushing up inflation for many countries, including UK and the US leading to higher prices for consumers.

Higher oil prices typically lead to petrol and diesel becoming more expensive.

While drivers are affected directly, households could also see prices of other goods, such as food, increase due to businesses passing on higher transportation costs to customers.

Inflation has fallen both in the UK - down to 2.6% in the year to June helped by slowing diesel and petrol prices - and in the US to 3.5%.

But questions remain whether the slow down will prove short-lived due to the renewed conflict in the Middle East.

New data released on Thursday showed that UK petrol prices have risen by 5p a litre since the beginning of July, hitting reaching almost £1.56.

Diesel is at £1.72 a litre, on average, according to the RAC.

Average gasoline prices in the US have surpassed $4 a gallon once more, up from $3.92 a month ago, according to motorist advocacy group AAA.

"More expensive fuel and energy can ripple through the wider economy, increasing costs for businesses and ultimately feeding through into the price of food and other goods," said Jonathan Raymond, investment manager at Quilter Cheviot.

"This creates another headache for central banks as they continue their battle against inflation.

"If energy prices remain elevated, policymakers may come under pressure to keep interest rates higher for longer or even raise them. This would come as a blow to mortgage holders and borrowers already feeling the strain."

FinanceTab.title: UK mortgage rates rise to highest level for more than a month
FinanceTab.text:
UK average mortgage rates have risen back to the level of a month ago as renewed tensions in the Middle East feed through to homeowners.

Lenders' funding costs have increased as markets judge that a prolonged conflict reduces the possibility of interest rate cuts by central banks.

The five biggest High Street banks are among a host of lenders which have increased their interest rates on new fixed deals in recent days.

Recent projections by the Bank of England suggest just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028.

Mortgage rates had been falling as a ceasefire between the US and Iran initially appeared to hold.

But fresh strikes and Houthi militia attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea reignited fears over global energy supplies.

Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May on Thursday after several days of increases, stoking fears of higher inflation and a lower likelihood of interest rate cuts.

More than eight in 10 mortgage customers have fixed-rate deals.

The interest rate on this kind of mortgage does not change until the deal expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it.

The average rate on a new two-year fixed deal is 5.59%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

Although it has risen consistently in recent days and is the highest since 19 June, it remains below the Iran war peak in April of 5.9%.

The average rate on a five-year fixed deal is 5.61%, a level last seen on 7 June.

HSBC has also announced it will raise its mortgage rates on Monday.

"It will be incredibly frustrating for borrowers to see rates rise back up to where they were a month ago. The positive progress over recent weeks now feels all but lost, but what the market needs is a period of stability," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts.

She said 100 deals had been pulled temporarily as lenders reconsider their pricing plans.

She suggested that anyone who needed to remortgage this year could lock in a new deal now with their existing lender ahead of time, but should also seek help from a broker to see whether there are better deals elsewhere.

"Brokers are an anchor during turbulent times as they can help borrowers keep abreast of changes and be there step by step when going through a mortgage application," she said.

Borrowers had been heartened by the regular falls in mortgage rates during June and early July, but brokers say the latest changes are evidence of the uncertainty in the sector.

"Any borrower hoping for rate cuts to become an ongoing trend will need to rethink," said David Hollingworth, of L&C Mortgages.

"Momentum has performed an about turn and now clearly shifted to fixed rates rising in the near term at least."

FinanceTab.title: We split money equally even when one of us earned a lot more
FinanceTab.text:
Hannah and Max have always split their money equally even when one has earned considerably more than the other.

"We've always wanted to do things 50/50," Max, 31, says. "We made a commitment to each other that what's mine is yours, and vice versa."

The couple got married after two years together, when Max was earning £70,000 a year working in tech, and Hannah, who works in the charity sector, was earning considerably less.

Their salaries go into a joint account and their mortgage, bills, food, petrol and other household costs are paid out of this.

Each month they take the same amount for personal spending.

If one of them wants to buy clothes, make-up or go to the pub they can do that without feeling watched and "it means we aren't accountable to each other for those things", says Max.

They also divide money into different pots, including savings and smaller funds for predictable spending like haircuts.

The pair came into the relationship with very different attitudes to money - Hannah's family discuss finances openly whereas for Max, "money was totally taboo".

"We never spoke about money so as an adult I was left without any knowledge of things like what's a good salary or how to negotiate my pay," he says.

When it came to buying a home together they had to be honest about how much they earned, how much they had for a deposit and what they could realistically afford.

"As first-time buyers, there are costs you don't think about, like stamp duty and solicitor fees, so it was important we both knew exactly how much money we had," Hannah says.

Now Hannah and Max say they make money an everyday conversation.

"Just this morning we were talking about what we can do to help improve our financial situation in the future," Hannah says.

Research from wealth manager Quilter suggests almost half of couples do not share financial planning equally, with 46% acting alone in some way and more than one in 10 leaving one partner solely responsible.

Relationship expert Karen Doherty has three pieces of advice when it comes to starting the conversation around financial planning.

The couple's system of sharing money remained the same even when Max was made redundant last year and they had to rely on Hannah's salary of between £40,000 and £60,000.

"There was shock and panic initially," Hannah, who did not want to disclose her precise salary, says. "But we sat down and really looked through where we could cut things out."

They cancelled gym memberships and Sky TV and went through their finances to make sure they could cover their mortgage and bills on a lower income.

Max had trained at culinary school instead of doing A-levels and university, but had moved away from hospitality because he felt it would not pay enough.

When he was made redundant he wanted to use the opportunity to create his own business in something he genuinely enjoyed - but Hannah had reservations.

"At first I told him to set this up alongside getting another job but we quickly realised the business would take a lot of time and energy," she says.

"We ran the numbers and decided that this was the right moment to take the risk given we don't have kids and no one else is depending on us."

Max spent £20,000 from his redundancy package buying and converting a horsebox trailer into a pizza truck, which now caters for weddings, parties and pop-ups.

He says the money he invested was their agreed limit to make the business work and if it failed he would find another job rather than putting in more.

The business now brings in between £4,000 and £6,000 a month in revenue and Max pays himself a salary that covers the mortgage.
